topic: Types And Architectures Of Ai Agents Sme

scenes.title: AI Agents: Action, Not Just Response
scenes.voiceover_narration: In the last topic, we established what an AI agent is: a system that doesn't just respond, but acts. We saw how agents take a goal, like monitoring site performance, and turn it into a sequence of real actions, from querying data to flagging anomalies.

scenes.title: Diverse Architectures & Learning Objectives
scenes.voiceover_narration: But not all agents work the same way. There are different types built on different architectures, designed for different kinds of problems. Understanding these differences allows you to match the right agent to the right job. By the end of this topic, you will describe the core components of an AI agent's architecture, explain agent-environment interaction, walk through the perception-reasoning-action cycle that drives agent decision making and identify the three main agent types, and one each as appropriate, as well as visualize how a complete agent workflow flows from input to outcome.

scenes.title: Core Components: Reasoning & Action
scenes.voiceover_narration: Then, there's the reasoning engine, typically an LLM, which interprets what the agent has perceived, decides what to do next, and determines which tools to use. decides what to do next, and determines which tools to use. Finally, the action layer. This is where the agent does something in the world: runs a query, calls an API, writes a file, or sends an alert. These four components work together in a continuous loop.

scenes.title: Agent-Environment Interaction Loop
scenes.voiceover_narration: That continuous loop—perceive, reason, act, then perceive again based on the result—is what we call agent-environment interaction. It separates an agent from a static tool. A static tool waits to be asked; an agent operates within an environment. It observes, decides, executes, then checks results and decides what comes next. This bi-directional relationship—where the environment shapes the agent, and the agent shapes the environment—makes agents useful in dynamic real-world contexts.

scenes.title: The Perception-Reasoning-Action Cycle
scenes.voiceover_narration: Let's slow that loop down and look at each stage. Perception is input. The agent receives information—a data reading, a user request, a tool result, or an error message. It takes that in and adds it to its working context. Reasoning is interpretation and planning. The agent's LLM processes what it's received, considers its goal, reviews what it's already done, and decides what action to take next. This is where the intelligence lives. Action is execution. The agent calls a tool, writes an output, sends a message, or updates a record. Something changes in the world as a result. Then the cycle begins again: the result of the action becomes new perception. The agent reasons about what that result means.

scenes.title: Types of Agents: Reactive & Goal-Based
scenes.voiceover_narration: Now let's talk about the three main types of agents. The first is the reactive agent. It responds to current input using predefined rules, with no memory or planning. Think of a simple Solara alert: if output drops below 8%, send a notification. Fast, predictable, but limited; it can't investigate why. The second type is the goal-based agent. This agent reasons about actions moving it closer to a defined outcome. It plans and evaluates options, choosing the path most likely to achieve its goal. Solara's Site Performance Investigation Agent works this way, deciding what data to pull based on what it finds to determine why a site under-performed.

scenes.title: Utility-Based Agents & Workflow
scenes.voiceover_narration: The third type is the utility-based agent. This agent asks: which available action achieves the goal most efficiently, at the lowest cost, and with the highest confidence? At Solara, a utility-based agent managing report generation across hundreds of sites makes trade-off decisions constantly: full diagnostic or summary? Escalate or log? It evaluates options against a utility function and picks the best one. Let's zoom out and look at how these components and concepts come together in a complete agent workflow. A goal arrives. The agent perceives it, adds it to context, and begins reasoning. It identifies the first action needed and executes. Results come back. The agent evaluates whether it's closer to the goal, plans the next action, and executes again. This continues until the goal is reached,

scenes.title: Handoff, Summary & What's Next
scenes.voiceover_narration: What's important is that workflow includes a handoff point. Good agent design always includes a point at which the agent recognizes the limits of its confidence and escalates. That's not a failure; it's responsible architecture. At Solara, an agent that flags an equipment anomaly it can't fully explain and routes it to a human engineer is doing exactly what it should. Let's bring it together. Every agent is built from four components: perception, memory, reasoning, and action, working in a continuous loop. That loop drives agent-environment interaction: observe, decide, act, observe again. The three types—reactive, goal-based, and utility-based—represent increasing sophistication. Coming up next, we're going hands-on. In the demo, we'll visualize types and architectures of AI agents in action, so you can see the decision loops and execution patterns running in real time. Let's take a look.
